reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / orbital disease literature
clinicalPearls: Inflammation of the lacrimal gland presenting with pain, swelling and redness over the outer third of the upper eyelid
The upper lid may take on a characteristic S-shaped contour from lateral gland enlargement
Acute dacryoadenitis is most often infective, classically viral (such as mumps or Epstein-Barr virus) or bacterial
Chronic or bilateral disease is more often non-infective, from sarcoidosis, IgG4-related disease, Sjogren syndrome or granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Fever, preauricular lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms point to an infective cause
Imaging and, in atypical or chronic cases, biopsy help distinguish infection from inflammatory or neoplastic disease
reference.pathophysiology: Dacryoadenitis is inflammation of the lacrimal gland that may be infective or non-infective. Acute infective dacryoadenitis follows viral or bacterial infection reaching the gland, producing acute painful enlargement with an inflammatory response. Non-infective forms arise from systemic granulomatous or autoimmune disease infiltrating the gland. The enlarged, inflamed gland displaces the globe and deforms the upper lid, and untreated bacterial infection can progress to abscess or orbital involvement.
additionalDifferentials: Lacrimal gland tumour (pleomorphic adenoma, lymphoma, carcinoma)
additionalInvestigations: Assessment for systemic infective features and preauricular nodes
CT or MRI of the orbit where the diagnosis is unclear or orbital extension is suspected
Viral and bacterial studies as clinically indicated
Serum IgG4, angiotensin-converting enzyme and autoimmune screen for chronic disease
Lacrimal gland biopsy for chronic, bilateral or mass-like presentations
redFlags: Proptosis, ophthalmoplegia or visual loss suggesting orbital extension
A firm mass or chronic painless enlargement suggesting tumour
Systemic features suggesting sarcoidosis or vasculitis
Failure to respond to appropriate treatment
reference.prognosis: Acute infective dacryoadenitis usually resolves with treatment of the underlying infection; prognosis of non-infective disease depends on the systemic condition, and a neoplastic cause must not be missed.
pitfalls: Assuming all lacrimal swelling is infective and missing a tumour or IgG4-related disease
Overlooking orbital extension of a bacterial infection
Failing to investigate chronic or bilateral disease for a systemic cause
Delaying biopsy of a suspicious mass
management: Treat bacterial acute dacryoadenitis with systemic antibiotics active against staphylococci and streptococci, together with warm compresses and analgesia
Manage viral dacryoadenitis, such as mumps or Epstein-Barr virus, supportively as it is usually self-limiting

Treat non-infective granulomatous or autoimmune disease according to the underlying cause, for example corticosteroids or immunosuppression for sarcoidosis, IgG4-related disease, Sjogren syndrome or granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Drain a lacrimal gland abscess surgically if one develops, and give intravenous antibiotics if orbital extension is suspected
Image the orbit with CT or MRI and biopsy chronic, bilateral or mass-like disease to exclude neoplasm and characterise inflammatory causes
Refer to oculoplastics and to the relevant specialist, such as rheumatology, for systemic disease
